title: Heredity and Genes
bigQuestion: How do instructions for building a living thing pass from parents to offspring, and why are offspring never exact copies?

story.title: The Monk Who Counted Peas
story.kicker: In a monastery garden, one patient man found the rules of heredity in thousands of pea plants.
paragraphs: In 1856, in the town of Brno in what is now the Czech Republic, a monk named Gregor Mendel walked out to a small garden beside the monastery wall. He had been a physics student. He liked numbers. He had a question that farmers had asked for centuries: why does a child look like its parents, and why does it sometimes not?

Mendel chose the garden pea. Peas are easy to grow, and each flower usually fertilizes itself, so a plant's offspring stay true year after year. He picked traits that came in two clear forms with nothing in between: round or wrinkled seeds, yellow or green seeds, tall or short stems, purple or white flowers. Then he did something almost no one had done before. He counted.

He crossed a true-breeding round-seeded plant with a true-breeding wrinkled one, brushing pollen from one flower onto another by hand. Every seed in the next generation was round. The wrinkled form had vanished. Then he let those plants fertilize themselves. Wrinkled seeds came back: 1,850 of them among 5,474 round ones. Almost exactly one in four.

He tried yellow and green, tall and short, one trait after another. The same pattern appeared every time: the hidden form disappeared for one generation, then returned in about one quarter of the next. Over eight years he grew and counted about 28,000 plants. In 1866 he published his results, and hardly anyone read them.

Mendel died in 1884, still mostly unknown as a scientist. In 1900, three biologists working separately found the same three-to-one ratio and then found Mendel's paper. The rules he uncovered in that garden are now the foundation of genetics. He had never seen a chromosome or a gene. He had only counted, carefully, and trusted the numbers.
story.think: Mendel's wrinkled trait vanished for one generation and then came back in one quarter of the plants. What might that tell you about how the instructions for a trait are stored and passed on?

lessons.title: Chromosomes and DNA
lessons.mainIdea: Every cell carries its instructions as DNA, packed into chromosomes, and each species has its own set.
reading: Look at a dividing onion root cell under the site's microscope at high power. Inside the nucleus, dark threads appear, line up and pull apart. These threads are *chromosomes*. Each one is a tightly coiled strand of *DNA*, a long molecule shaped like a twisted ladder. The rungs of the ladder are pairs of four chemical bases, usually written A, T, C and G. The order of those letters is the instruction.

Your body cells each hold 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. One chromosome of each pair came from your mother and one from your father. Dogs have 78. Fruit flies have 8. The pea plants Mendel grew have 14. The number does not measure how complex an organism is; it is just how that species packages its DNA.

The instructions are astonishingly long. All the DNA in one human cell holds about 3 billion base pairs. Stretched out, it would be about 2 meters long, yet it fits inside a nucleus far too small to see without a microscope. When a cell divides, it copies every chromosome first, so each new cell gets a full set.

words.d: a tightly coiled strand of DNA inside a cell's nucleus that carries many genes
the long twisted-ladder molecule whose sequence of bases holds the instructions for a living thing
the part of a cell that holds the chromosomes

look.title: Chromosome Counts in Body Cells
look.prompt: A dog has more chromosomes than a human. Does that mean a dog is more complex? What does the count actually tell you?

check.q: Chromosomes are made of:
check.why: Each chromosome is one long DNA molecule coiled up tightly with proteins.

check.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
check.why: Humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent.

check.q: What carries the actual instruction in DNA?
choices: The order of the four bases
check.why: The sequence of A, T, C and G is the code. Different orders mean different instructions.

lessons.title: Genes Build Proteins
lessons.mainIdea: A gene is a stretch of DNA that tells a cell how to build one protein, and proteins do the work that gives an organism its traits.
reading: A chromosome is like a long book. A *gene* is one recipe in that book: a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for building one *protein*. Proteins are the working molecules of a cell. Some are building blocks, like the collagen in your skin and the keratin in your hair. Some are tools, like the enzymes that break down your lunch. Some carry signals, like insulin.

Here is how the recipe becomes a trait. A cell reads a gene and links together a chain of small units called amino acids in the order the gene spells out. The chain folds into a protein with a specific shape. That shape decides what the protein can do. A pea plant with a working gene for a starch-building enzyme makes round seeds. If that enzyme does not form correctly, the seed dries out wrinkled. Mendel's round and wrinkled traits come down to one protein.

Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes. Your eye color, your blood type, whether you can digest milk as an adult, and how your body handles some medicines all trace back to which versions of certain genes you carry and which proteins they build. Many traits, like height, depend on hundreds of genes working together plus food and environment.

words.d: a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for building one protein
a working molecule built by a cell from a gene's instructions; proteins build structures and do jobs in the body
a feature of an organism, like seed shape or eye color
a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in a living thing

look.title: One Broken Recipe
look.text: Two pea seeds sit on the bench. One is smooth and round. One is shrunken and wrinkled. Inside the round seed, an enzyme has turned sugar into starch, which holds water well. Inside the wrinkled seed, the gene for that enzyme has a change in it. The enzyme never forms properly. Less starch is made, more water is lost as the seed dries, and the seed coat collapses.
look.prompt: Trace the chain from gene to trait for the wrinkled seed. Which step changed first, and which step is the trait you can see?

check.q: A gene is best described as:
choices: The instructions for building one protein
check.why: A gene is one stretch of DNA that codes for one protein. A chromosome holds many genes.

check.q: Which of these is a protein?
check.why: Enzymes are proteins. They are built from amino acids using a gene's instructions.

check.q: Why does a change in a gene often change a trait?
choices: Because genes are made of protein
Because the protein it builds may change shape and stop working
Because the cell loses its nucleus
check.why: The protein's shape depends on the gene's sequence, and shape decides what the protein can do.

lessons.title: Dominant and Recessive
lessons.mainIdea: Each organism carries two copies of most genes, and a dominant version can hide a recessive one for a generation.
reading: Mendel's peas carried a secret he could not see. Each plant has two copies of the gene for seed shape, one on each chromosome of a pair. Different versions of a gene are called *alleles*. Call the round allele R and the wrinkled allele r. A plant with two R alleles, RR, makes round seeds. A plant with rr makes wrinkled seeds. A plant with Rr makes round seeds too, because one working enzyme gene is enough.

The allele that shows even when only one copy is present is *dominant*. The one that hides is *recessive*. When Mendel crossed RR with rr, every offspring got one R and one r. All were Rr, and all were round. The wrinkled allele had not vanished. It was riding along, hidden.

When Rr plants fertilized themselves, each parent passed on either R or r, at random. The offspring could be RR, Rr, rR or rr, each equally likely. Three of those four combinations contain at least one R and look round. One is rr and looks wrinkled. Three to one. Mendel's ratio was not magic. It was two alleles per plant, one passed on by each parent, sorted by chance.

words.d: one version of a gene; for example, the round allele or the wrinkled allele for seed shape
an allele that shows its trait even when only one copy is present
an allele whose trait shows only when both copies are that allele

look.title: Mendel's Counts in the Second Generation
look.cite: Gregor Mendel, Experiments on Plant Hybrids, 1866
look.prompt: Divide the larger number by the smaller in each pair. What ratio do you get? Why is it close to, but not exactly, three to one?

check.q: A pea plant with alleles Rr makes round seeds. This shows that the round allele is:
check.why: A dominant allele shows its trait even when paired with a different allele.

check.q: What must a plant's alleles be if it makes wrinkled seeds?
check.why: The recessive trait appears only when both copies are the recessive allele.

check.q: Why did the wrinkled trait disappear in Mendel's first generation and return in the second?
choices: The wrinkled allele was hidden by the dominant allele and then paired up again by chance
The plants forgot how to be wrinkled
The wrinkled allele was destroyed and then rebuilt
check.why: All first-generation plants were Rr and looked round. Their offspring could be rr, which shows the hidden trait.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Reproduce
lessons.mainIdea: Asexual reproduction copies one parent exactly, while sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents and creates variation.
reading: Snap a stem off a spider plant, put it in water, and roots grow. The new plant is a copy of the old one, with identical DNA. This is *asexual reproduction*: one parent, no mixing, offspring that are clones. Bacteria split in two this way. So do hydras, some lizards and many plants. It is fast, and it works well when conditions are stable.

Most animals and plants also reproduce sexually. In *sexual reproduction*, each parent makes special cells, egg or sperm in animals, that carry only one chromosome from each pair. In humans that is 23. When egg and sperm join, the offspring gets 46: half from each parent. Which chromosome of each pair ends up in a given egg or sperm is random, so every child of the same parents gets a different mix.

That mixing creates *variation*, differences among individuals. Two siblings share parents but not the same combination of alleles. Variation is why a family's children look alike but never identical, unless they are identical twins from one fertilized egg. It also matters for survival. If a new disease strikes, a population with variation is more likely to include some individuals that resist it.

words.d: reproduction from one parent that makes offspring with the same DNA as the parent
reproduction in which two parents each give half the chromosomes, making offspring with a new mix
differences among individuals of the same species

look.title: The Potato Blight
look.text: In the 1840s most of Ireland's potatoes were one variety, grown by planting pieces of last year's potatoes rather than seeds. Every plant was a clone with the same DNA. When a fungus-like disease arrived, it spread through fields with almost nothing to slow it, and the harvests failed for several years in a row.
look.prompt: Why was a crop of clones so vulnerable? How might a field of potatoes grown from seed, with variation, have fared differently?

check.q: Which is an example of asexual reproduction?
choices: A hen laying a fertilized egg
A pea flower fertilized by another pea plant
check.why: One bacterium splits into two identical cells with no mixing of genes.

check.q: A human egg cell carries how many chromosomes?
check.why: Egg and sperm each carry one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs. Joined, they make 46.

check.q: What is the main advantage of sexual reproduction for a population?
choices: It is faster than asexual reproduction
It creates variation that helps some individuals survive changes
check.why: Mixing genes from two parents produces varied offspring, so some are likely to cope with new conditions.

lessons.title: The Punnett Square
lessons.mainIdea: A Punnett square lists every possible combination of alleles from two parents and shows how likely each one is.
reading: Around 1905, an English geneticist named Reginald Punnett drew a simple grid to keep track of Mendel's crosses. It is still used today. Write one parent's two alleles across the top and the other parent's two alleles down the side. Fill each box with one allele from the top and one from the side. The four boxes show every possible offspring.

Try a cross of two Rr plants. Across the top: R, r. Down the side: R, r. The boxes read RR, Rr, Rr, rr. Three boxes hold at least one R, so three quarters of the offspring are expected to be round. One box is rr, so one quarter are expected to be wrinkled. That is Mendel's three-to-one ratio drawn as a picture.

Now try Rr crossed with rr. The boxes read Rr, Rr, rr, rr. Half round, half wrinkled. The *Punnett square* does not tell you what any single seed will be. It tells you the chances. An organism with two identical alleles, like RR or rr, is *homozygous*. One with two different alleles, like Rr, is *heterozygous*. A heterozygous plant looks like a homozygous dominant one, but it carries the hidden allele.

words.d: a grid that shows all possible allele combinations from two parents and their chances
having two identical alleles for a gene, such as RR or rr
having two different alleles for a gene, such as Rr

look.title: The Cat Cross
look.text: In cats, a short coat is dominant over a long coat. A shelter has a short-haired mother cat that had one long-haired parent, so she carries one allele for each. The father is long-haired. Her litter has five kittens. Draw the grid before you answer.
look.prompt: What fraction of the kittens would you expect to have long hair? Could all five turn out short-haired? Explain.

check.q: In a Punnett square for Rr crossed with Rr, how many of the four boxes show the recessive trait?
check.why: Only the rr box shows the recessive trait; the other three contain a dominant R.

check.q: A plant with alleles Rr is called:
check.why: Two different alleles for one gene make an organism heterozygous.

check.q: Cross an Rr plant with an rr plant. What fraction of offspring is expected to be wrinkled?
check.why: The boxes are Rr, Rr, rr, rr. Two of four are rr, so half are expected to be wrinkled.

lessons.title: Chance, Not Certainty
lessons.mainIdea: Genetic ratios are probabilities; they describe many offspring on average, not what any single one must be.
reading: Flip a coin four times. You expect two heads, but you might get four, or none. Each flip is separate. Alleles work the same way. A Punnett square for Rr times Rr predicts one wrinkled seed in four. A single pod with six seeds might hold zero wrinkled seeds, or three. Only when you count thousands, as Mendel did, does the count settle close to the prediction.

This is why Mendel's numbers were 5,474 to 1,850, not exactly 5,475 to 1,825. *Probability* tells you the chance of each outcome, not the result of any one event. A couple who each carry one allele for a recessive condition has a one-in-four chance with each child. Having one child with the condition does not lower the chance for the next. Each fertilization is a new coin flip.

Understanding chance protects you from a common mistake. People sometimes say a trait "skipped a generation." It did not skip anything. A recessive allele was carried, hidden, by heterozygous parents. When two carriers happened to pass it on together, the trait appeared. Chance decided when, not any plan.

words.d: the chance that something will happen, often written as a fraction or percent
a heterozygous individual who carries a recessive allele without showing its trait

look.title: Two Pods
look.text: A student opens two pods from Rr plants. Pod 1 has seven seeds: five round, two wrinkled. Pod 2 has five seeds: all round. Her partner says the Punnett square must be wrong because neither pod shows a three-to-one ratio.
look.prompt: Is the partner right? What would you tell her about chance, and how many seeds would you want to count before judging the prediction?

check.q: Two carrier parents have a child with a recessive condition. The chance for their next child is:
check.why: Each fertilization is independent. The one-in-four chance is the same every time.

check.q: Why did Mendel need thousands of plants to see the three-to-one pattern clearly?
choices: Small samples vary a lot by chance; large ones settle near the expected ratio
Peas only show traits in big fields
He was paid by the plant
Small samples always show exactly three to one
check.why: Probability describes averages over many events, so large counts come closer to the prediction.

check.q: A trait seems to "skip a generation." What really happened?
choices: The gene disappeared and came back
The trait was caused by weather
The allele was not in the family until it was reinvented
A recessive allele was carried by heterozygous parents and then paired up
check.why: The allele never left. It was hidden in carriers until two copies met by chance in one offspring.

lessons.title: What a Mutation Is
lessons.mainIdea: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence, and it can come from copying mistakes or from damage by chemicals or radiation.
reading: Every time a cell divides, it copies about 3 billion base pairs. The copying machinery is remarkably accurate, and repair enzymes fix most slips, but a few errors get through. A single base may be swapped for another, dropped or added. Any change in the DNA sequence is a *mutation*. Ultraviolet light from the sun, some chemicals in tobacco smoke, and radiation can also damage DNA and cause mutations.

Where a mutation happens matters. A mutation in a skin cell affects only that cell and the cells that grow from it. It cannot be passed to children. A mutation in an egg or sperm cell can be passed on, and then every cell of the offspring will carry it. Mendel's wrinkled allele began, long ago, as a mutation in one pea plant that got passed down.

Most mutations change one letter among billions. Many land in stretches of DNA that do not code for any protein, so nothing happens. Others change one amino acid in a protein. Sometimes that makes no difference to the protein's shape. Sometimes it ruins it. Sometimes, rarely, it makes the protein work better in a new way. Mutations are the ultimate source of every new allele.

words.d: a change in the sequence of bases in DNA
energy such as ultraviolet light or X-rays that can damage DNA
the order of the bases along a strand of DNA

look.title: A Copying Slip
look.text: Imagine a sentence copied by hand a million times: THE CAT ATE THE RAT. In one copy the T in CAT became an H: THE CHAT ATE THE RAT. In another, a letter was dropped: THE CAT ATE TH RAT. In a third, a change landed in the blank space between words, and the sentence reads the same as before.
look.prompt: Match each copy to a kind of mutation: one that changes meaning, one that breaks meaning, and one that changes nothing. Why are all three still called mutations?

check.q: A mutation is:
choices: A change in the DNA sequence
Any change in an animal's behavior
A disease caused by a virus
check.why: Mutation means a change in the order of bases in DNA, whatever effect it has.

check.q: Which mutation could be passed on to a person's children?
choices: One in a sperm or egg cell
One caused by sunburn on the arm
check.why: Only mutations in the cells that form the next generation, egg and sperm, are inherited.

check.q: What happens to most single-letter mutations?
choices: They have little or no effect
check.why: Many land where they change nothing, or change a protein so slightly that it still works.

lessons.title: Harmful, Helpful, Neutral
lessons.mainIdea: Whether a mutation is harmful, helpful or neutral depends on what it does to a protein and on the environment the organism lives in.
reading: Consider one famous mutation. A single base change in the gene for hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, swaps one amino acid. With two copies of this allele, a person's red blood cells can bend into a stiff sickle shape, block small blood vessels and cause pain and organ damage. This is sickle cell disease. In that form, the mutation is clearly *harmful*.

Yet the same allele is common in parts of Africa, India and the Mediterranean where malaria is widespread. People with one sickle allele and one normal allele are mostly healthy, and they are much less likely to die of severe malaria. In a place with malaria, carrying one copy is *helpful*. In a place without it, the allele gives no benefit. Helpful and harmful are not fixed labels. They depend on the environment.

Another example is closer to lunch. Most mammals stop making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, after infancy. Thousands of years ago, mutations arose in some human populations that keep the lactase gene switched on into adulthood. Where people herded cattle and drank milk, this allele spread. Where they did not, it stayed rare.

Most mutations are *neutral*: they change nothing you can measure. Your DNA differs from a classmate's at millions of positions, and nearly all of those differences have no effect at all. Neutral changes still matter to scientists. They pile up at a steady pace and can be used, like a clock, to estimate how long ago two populations or two species separated.

words.d: a mutation that makes an organism less likely to survive or reproduce in its environment
a mutation that makes an organism more likely to survive or reproduce in its environment
a mutation that has no measurable effect on the organism
the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen

look.title: Understanding Sickle Cell
look.text: Government health agencies explain that sickle cell disease is inherited, that a person must receive a sickle cell gene from both parents to have the disease, and that a person who receives the gene from only one parent has sickle cell trait, which usually causes no symptoms.
look.cite: U.S. National Institutes of Health and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, public health information, paraphrased
look.prompt: Using the words dominant, recessive and carrier, explain why a person with one sickle allele is usually healthy.

check.q: Why is the sickle cell allele common in regions with malaria?
choices: Having one copy protects against severe malaria
Malaria mosquitoes avoid people with two copies
check.why: Carriers survive malaria better, so the allele stays common even though two copies cause disease.

check.q: The same allele can be helpful in one place and useless in another. This shows that:
choices: Whether a mutation helps depends on the environment
Alleles change depending on the weather
check.why: A mutation's effect on survival depends on the conditions the organism faces.

check.q: Most differences between your DNA and a classmate's are:
check.why: Nearly all of the millions of differences between people have no measurable effect.

lessons.title: Selective Breeding
lessons.mainIdea: For thousands of years people have chosen which plants and animals reproduce, and that choice slowly reshapes a species.
reading: Drive through Illinois in August and you see corn to the horizon. Its ancestor was a wild grass from Mexico called teosinte, with tiny ears of a few hard kernels. Over thousands of years, farmers saved seed from the plants with the biggest, softest kernels and planted those. Generation by generation, the ears grew. This is *selective breeding*: humans choosing which individuals reproduce based on the traits they want.

Selective breeding does not create new alleles. It works on the variation that mutation and sexual reproduction already provide. A farmer cannot choose a trait that no plant in the field shows. But by breeding only the plants that lean the right way, the farmer makes the wanted alleles more common. Every dog breed, from Chihuahua to Great Dane, came from wolves this way. Cabbage, broccoli, kale and Brussels sprouts were all bred from one wild mustard plant.

There are trade-offs. Breeding for one trait can drag others along. Some dog breeds bred for a flat face struggle to breathe. Crop varieties bred for yield can lose disease resistance, which is why seed banks store older varieties. Illinois is home to a long-running corn experiment at the University of Illinois that has selected corn for high and low oil content every year since 1896, and the two lines still keep moving apart.

words.d: choosing which plants or animals reproduce so that wanted traits become more common
the wild grass from Mexico that farmers bred into corn
a group within a species, like a dog breed, shaped by selective breeding

look.title: Choosing the Seed
look.text: A gardener grows fifty tomato plants from the same seed packet. They vary: some fruits are sweet, some sour, some large, some small. She saves seed only from the three sweetest plants and grows those next year. She repeats this for ten years. By the end, nearly every plant is sweet, but the fruits are smaller and the plants get a leaf disease more often.
look.prompt: Explain how the gardener changed the tomatoes without adding any new alleles. What trade-off appeared, and why?

check.q: Selective breeding works by:
choices: Creating brand-new alleles in a lab
Letting only individuals with wanted traits reproduce
check.why: Breeders choose parents with the traits they want, making those alleles more common over generations.

check.q: Corn was bred from:
check.why: Farmers in Mexico slowly bred teosinte, a grass with tiny ears, into modern corn.

check.q: Which is a trade-off of selective breeding?
choices: It needs no variation to work
Breeding for one trait can bring unwanted traits along
check.why: Selecting hard for one trait can drag along others, like breathing trouble in flat-faced dogs.

lessons.title: Genetic Engineering
lessons.mainIdea: Genetic engineering moves or edits genes directly, which is faster and more precise than breeding and raises new questions.
reading: Before the 1980s, people with diabetes relied on insulin taken from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Then scientists cut the human insulin gene out of human DNA and pasted it into bacteria. The bacteria read the gene and built human insulin. It was approved for patients in 1982, and most insulin is made this way today. This is *genetic engineering*: changing an organism's DNA directly, often by adding a gene from another species.

Farmers use it too. Much of the corn grown in Illinois carries a gene from a soil bacterium that makes a protein toxic to certain caterpillars but not to people. Other crops carry genes that let them survive a weed killer. Newer tools such as CRISPR let scientists edit a gene in place, changing a few letters rather than adding a whole gene from elsewhere.

Genetic engineering is far faster than breeding and can move genes between species that could never breed. That power brings questions. Could an engineered gene spread to wild relatives? Are edited foods safe to eat? Who should own a gene? Scientists test engineered crops for years before approval, and the evidence so far shows approved foods are as safe as conventional ones, but debate about rules, labels and uses continues.

Compare the two methods with a pea plant. A breeder wanting a disease-resistant pea searches thousands of plants for one that resists, then crosses for years. An engineer finds the resistance gene, perhaps in a wild pea, and inserts it in one season. Both rely on the same fact: a gene is a recipe, and a cell will follow a recipe it is given.

words.d: changing an organism's DNA directly, often by adding or editing a gene
a protein hormone that controls blood sugar; people with diabetes may need to take it
a tool that lets scientists edit a gene in place inside a living cell

look.title: Two Paths to the Same Pea
look.text: A seed company wants a pea that resists a fungus. Team A screens 20,000 plants, finds three resistant ones, and crosses them with high-yield plants for six years until the resistance is stable. Team B finds the resistance gene in a wild pea and inserts it into the high-yield variety in one year. Team B's pea must then pass several years of safety tests before sale.
look.prompt: List one advantage and one drawback of each path. Why might a farmer or a shopper prefer one over the other?

check.q: How is most human insulin for patients made today?
choices: By bacteria carrying the human insulin gene
check.why: The human insulin gene was inserted into bacteria, which read it and build the protein.

check.q: What can genetic engineering do that selective breeding cannot?
choices: Move a gene between species that cannot breed together
check.why: Breeding only mixes alleles within a species. Engineering can add a gene from any organism.

check.q: Which statement about engineered crops is accurate?
choices: They are never tested before sale
Scientists test them for years, and debate about rules continues
They were first sold in the 1800s
check.why: Engineered crops go through years of safety testing, while questions about use and labeling are still discussed.

lessons.title: Reading the Whole Book
lessons.mainIdea: The Human Genome Project read the entire sequence of human DNA, giving scientists a map for finding genes linked to health and disease.
reading: In 1990 scientists in the United States and several other countries set out to read every base of human DNA, all 3 billion letters. The effort, called the Human Genome Project, took thirteen years and thousands of researchers. In 2003 they announced the sequence was essentially complete. A *genome* is an organism's entire set of DNA. Reading it is like getting the whole cookbook instead of one recipe.

The map surprised people. Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, far fewer than many had guessed, and about the same number as a mouse. Only a small fraction of the genome codes for proteins. Much of the rest controls when and where genes are switched on. Two unrelated people share about 99.9 percent of their sequence.

Since then, the cost of reading a genome has dropped from billions of dollars to a few hundred, and reading takes days instead of years. Doctors can now find the exact mutation behind some rare diseases in a child. Researchers compare genomes across species to trace how genes changed over time. The same map also raises questions about privacy and who may see your genetic information, questions that laws are still catching up with.

words.d: the complete set of DNA in an organism
the international effort, 1990 to 2003, to read the full sequence of human DNA

look.title: What the Project Set Out to Do
look.text: The National Human Genome Research Institute describes the Human Genome Project as an international research effort, begun in 1990 and completed in 2003, whose goal was to determine the sequence of the human genome and identify the genes it contains, and to make that information freely available to researchers.
look.cite: National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH, project overview, paraphrased
look.prompt: Why might it matter that the sequence was made freely available instead of kept by one company?

check.q: A genome is:
choices: An organism's complete set of DNA
check.why: The genome is all the DNA in an organism, every chromosome and every gene.

check.q: About how many protein-coding genes do humans have?
check.why: Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes. Three billion is the number of base pairs, not genes.

check.q: Which is a result of the Human Genome Project?
choices: Doctors can find the exact mutation behind some rare diseases
check.why: With the full sequence as a map, researchers can compare a patient's DNA and find disease-causing changes.

review.q: The order of bases in DNA:
choices: Is the same in every species
Carries the instructions for building proteins
Changes every time a cell divides
review.why: The sequence of A, T, C and G spells out the recipes for proteins, which produce traits.

review.q: Two Rr pea plants are crossed. What fraction of offspring is expected to make wrinkled seeds?
review.why: The boxes RR, Rr, Rr, rr include one rr, so one in four is expected to be wrinkled.

review.q: A plant with alleles Rr has round seeds. Which term describes it?
review.why: Two different alleles make it heterozygous. It shows the dominant trait but carries the recessive allele.

review.q: Which reproduction creates the most variation among offspring?
choices: A plant grown from a cutting
review.why: Sexual reproduction mixes chromosomes from two parents in random combinations.
Only mutations in egg or sperm cells pass to the next generation.

review.q: One sickle cell allele helps people survive malaria. This shows that a mutation's effect:
choices: Depends on the size of the chromosome
review.why: The same allele is helpful where malaria is common and offers no advantage where it is not.

review.q: Selective breeding and genetic engineering are alike because both:
choices: Change which alleles an organism carries
review.why: Both change the genes a population carries, though breeding is slower and engineering can move genes between species.

review.q: The Human Genome Project found that humans have about:
review.why: Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, fewer than many scientists expected.
